newsitem.title: USA: Lower rates, improved confidence boost US housing.
newsitem.headline: Lower rates, improved confidence boost US housing.

text.p: Lower rates helped bolster U.S. housing starts in June, but the most notable gains were evident in the multifamily sector, economists said.
As reported, June housing starts rose 4.8 percent to a 1.452 million unit annual rate, and the multi-family sector saw a 12.9 percent leap.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had expected June starts to rise to 1.45 million.
Lower rates and improved consumer confidence bolstered starts, according to Dan Seto, economist with The Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
"Housing starts were better than expected," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.

Lieberman noted that poor weather dampened May housing activity and some of the vigor in the latest report may in fact be a rebound from that weather effect. "There was a weather problem last month and we have rebounded some from that. The weather has been a distinct problem," he said.
Lieberman pointed out that the regional mix of activity was "odd," adding that the Northeast saw a decline in housing activity, "whereas all other parts of the country were better."
As reported, the Northeastern U.S. saw a 6.6-percent decline in housing starts.
Lieberman said housing starts likely will linger between an annualized rate of 1.45 million and 1.5 million.
One economist tempered the import of lower rates on housing starts.
Morton Swinksy, president and chief executive officer at Fuji Securities, said that with lower rates, housing starts "will get some degree of a boost.
Seto of Nikko characterized the 2.6-percent decline in June permits as temporary.
"The permits number fell, but this is not a continued omen for softening," he added.
John Mcauley, economist at Wilkinson Boyd Capital Markets, said the housing industry has seen more strength than was expected.

While the single-family component has been buoyed by consumer demand, the overall data have been propelled by a firm tone in multi-family housing, he noted. "I think the single-family component is softer than the overall number," but there is "good consumer-type demand," he said.

Mcauley noted that the multi-family sector was enjoying strong institutional type of investment -- meaning developers were taking advantage of lower borrowing costs to bring in new multi-family supply.

Mcauley said that while rates were an incentive for consumers in the single-family sector, confidence was also behind the increase in activity. "There are favorable fundamentals for households ... employment, prospects for wage growth ..."

Nikko's Seto agreed that consumer confidence has improved nationwide. "Clearly housing is still strong and signals ongoing strength. At this stage, I don't think it will lead to any inflation worries."
Swinksy also believes the strength in housing starts does not portend inflation. The strength, he said, is "not necessarily inflation."
